issues.detail: Examples are Express/TypeScript-specific despite claiming compatibility with Python 3.9+ and Go 1.21+; Python and Go developers would need to translate the TypeScript implementation to their frameworks.

scenarios.name: multi-tier-endpoint-limits
scenarios.rationale: Response A meets all rubric requirements: defines three tiers with correct configs, sets X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers on all responses, and uses IP-based keys for auth/public and user ID-based for data. Response B fails two critical requirements: it sets RFC standard RateLimit-* headers (not X-RateLimit-*) due to standardHeaders/legacyHeaders config, and the auth endpoint keys on username/email instead of IP-based.

scenarios.name: credential-stuffing-detection
scenarios.rationale: Response A fully satisfies the rubric by using Redis SET for cardinality counting, enforcing the 10-username/5-min threshold, and returning 429 with Retry-After. Response B implements a clean NestJS solution with threshold and 429 responses but critically fails the rubric's explicit requirement to use a Redis data structure—it uses in-memory Map/Set instead and only mentions Redis as a future upgrade.

scenarios.name: redis-fallback-in-memory
scenarios.rationale: Both meet the rubric's three requirements (try-catch with fallback, logging, strict enforcement). Response A uses sliding-window counters in both Redis (ZSET) and memory, providing more accurate rate limiting with distributed consistency via server time, plus active health checks and memory cleanup. Response B uses simpler fixed-window counters (INCR + PEXPIRE) that allow boundary-window request slips, lacks in-memory cleanup, and has no recovery health checks, though it is more readable and includes useful operational endpoints.
